title: How to Build a Knowledge Base with Permissions and Approvals
summary: Learn how to build a knowledge base in seven steps, with access permissions, version control, approval workflows, testing and ongoing content reviews.
body_markdown:
To build a knowledge base, define its audience, organize trusted content, connect source data, configure permissions, establish approval rules, test the publishing process, and schedule maintenance. A searchable answer is not useful if it is outdated, unapproved, or visible to the wrong person.


A knowledge base is an organized collection of answers, instructions, and policies. An **internal knowledge base** serves employees; a customer-facing one supports external users. Either can supply an AI assistant, but AI retrieval requires additional permission and answer-quality checks.


This guide explains how to build a knowledge base when audience restrictions, existing data, or controlled updates matter. For a small collection of public, low-risk answers, a simpler publishing process may suffice. Use the controls your content requires—not complexity for its own sake.


The architecture below is a recommended design. Jet Admin’s supplied use-case descriptions illustrate relevant building blocks, not a verified, preconfigured implementation.


> **Key Takeaways** Start with one audience, authoritative sources, and questions you can test.Control data and actions, not just visible screens.Approve an immutable revision, including its reader-facing metadata.Keep the published answer available while its replacement is reviewed.Test access boundaries and assign ongoing content ownership before rollout.


## Step 1 — Define the audience, questions, and success criteria


Choose a bounded scope, such as “approved troubleshooting guidance for frontline support,” rather than “all company knowledge.”


Collect representative questions from support conversations or employee requests. For each, record the expected answer, authoritative source, intended audience, accountable owner, and sensitivity. Define what happens when no reliable answer exists.


Measure success through **findability, correctness, and access compliance** : can an intended reader locate the current answer, and can an unauthorized person retrieve any part of it?


### Write a minimum viable knowledge base specification


Requirement What to document


Audience Initial reader group and excluded audiences


Content scope Included questions, sensitive categories, and exclusions


Sources Authoritative documents, databases, and attachment storage


Roles Readers, authors, reviewers, publishers, and access administrators


Publishing states Draft, in review, approved, published, and retired


Ownership Content, technical, and access-control responsibilities


Acceptance criteria Expected answers and required access and publishing tests


Decide whether AI answers are necessary. Ordinary browsing and search may satisfy the initial scope. If you add AI, determine how permissions and published-revision boundaries will apply before content reaches the model.


**Acceptance check:** Every launch question has an expected answer, source, audience, and owner.


## Step 2 — Connect source data and define permissions


Audit sources before connecting them. Resolve conflicting policies, remove duplicates, identify obsolete material, and assign missing owners. Importing content does not make it approved.


Define knowledge base permissions along two dimensions:


- **Content scope:** Which organizations, departments, articles, and fields may someone access?
- **Actions:** May they read, edit, submit, approve, publish, or retire content?


### Create a role-and-action matrix


This matrix is a proposed design—not a description of default Jet Admin roles.


Role Read Edit Submit Approve Publish or retire


Reader Authorized published content No No No No


Author Authorized content and assigned drafts Assigned drafts Assigned drafts No No


Reviewer Assigned review scope Comments only No Assigned fixed revisions No


Publisher Assigned publishing scope No content edits No Only if separately authorized Within scope


An access administrator separately manages identity mappings and access policies. Where separation of duties matters, prevent authors from approving their own changes.


**Hiding a button is not authorization.** Enforce restrictions in data queries and action execution, including direct requests, attachments, and exports.


Jet Admin’s[Knowledge Base use case](https://www.jetadmin.io/use-cases/knowledge-base?ref=jetadmin.io) describes hubs over existing Postgres, MySQL, or Mongo data. It lists row- and column-level permissions, SSO, audit logs, and deployment on Jet Cloud, in a customer cloud account, or on-premise. It does not establish built-in article search or approvals.


Resolve four prerequisites before building:


1. **Storage:** Where will articles, revisions, approvals, and files live?
2. **Identity:** Which identity provider supplies reliable user and organization membership?
3. **Enforcement:** Which backend, database policies, or service checks authorize each operation?
4. **Implementation ownership:** Who builds and tests controls the selected configuration does not provide?


Confirm SSO, logging, permission enforcement, and deployment availability for your intended plan rather than treating the use-case description as a plan-level guarantee.


**Acceptance check:** Each role has explicit scope and actions; unspecified access is denied.


## Step 3 — Define ownership, versions, and the publishing lifecycle


Keep article identity separate from approved content. Otherwise, editing a title, audience, or attachment could change what readers receive without review.


Use this proposed model:


Record Fields and purpose


Article Stable ID, published-revision reference, operational owner, next-review date


Revision Revision ID, article ID, title, body, category, navigation labels, tags, synonyms, intended audience, source references, versioned attachment references, author, state


Approval Exact revision ID, reviewer, decision, timestamp, comments


Governance event Actor, authorized ownership or access-policy change, timestamp, reason


### Separate working revisions from published content


Use one consistent rule: **any change to the approved content snapshot requires a new draft and renewed approval.** This includes corrections, titles, categories, audience assignments, and attachment replacements—not just substantive body edits.


Submitted revisions are immutable. If changes are requested, create a successor draft and preserve the reviewed snapshot and decision.


```text
Draft → In review → Approved → Published → Retired
│
└─ Changes requested → New draft → New review


Published revision A ───────────────→ Readers
│
└─ Replacement draft B → Review → Approval
│
Atomic publication
│
Readers receive B


```


*The current published revision remains available while its replacement is prepared.*


Operational changes, such as assigning an owner or rescheduling a review, need separate authorization and logging but not content approval. They must not alter reader-visible content or grant access. A rescheduled review date is not evidence that content was reviewed.


Keep live access-policy administration separate from content editing. Authorized administrators can revoke access immediately. Changes that broaden eligibility need explicit access authorization; changing a revision’s intended audience also requires renewed content approval. Readers must satisfy both the approved audience scope and current access policy.


The[Build Document Management Software use case](https://www.jetadmin.io/use-cases/document-management-software?ref=jetadmin.io) describes versions, owners, retention, approval, retirement, and serving approved versions while retaining history. Per-user read acknowledgement is relevant where policies require it.


Knowledge base version control is distinct from app-builder history: restoring a screen does not establish which text was approved.


**Acceptance check:** Editing any replacement content or reader-facing metadata leaves the published snapshot unchanged.


## Step 4 — Build the reading and authoring experience


Give readers a clear route to answers and contributors a separate route to managing them.


Start with information architecture:


- Group content around reader tasks, such as “Request access,” rather than internal team names.
- Use a small, distinct set of categories with clear navigation labels.
- Maintain controlled tags; avoid several labels for the same concept.
- Record user vocabulary and synonyms, such as “sign in” and “login.”
- Test whether readers can choose the right category without knowing your organization chart.


Use a consistent article template: question-led title, direct answer, steps, exceptions, escalation route, and source. Show a last-reviewed date only when a completed review supports it.


Plan an article view, navigation, editor, and review queue. Treat search, synonym handling, filters, attachments, and permission-filtered results as requirements to implement and validate—not assumed features.


### Turn the requirements into a build-ready prompt


If you use an AI builder, provide a specification such as:


> Build an internal support knowledge base on our selected content database and attachment storage. Use our identity provider’s user and group mappings.
>
>
> Separate Article, Revision, Approval, and Governance Event records. Include revision-controlled titles, bodies, categories, tags, synonyms, audiences, sources, and attachment versions. Keep operational ownership and review scheduling separately authorized.
>
>
> Create distinct reader and contributor experiences using the agreed role matrix. Support draft, in-review, approved, published, and retired states. Submitted snapshots must be immutable; changed content requires a new draft and approval.
>
>
> Build task-based navigation, article views, an editor, and a review queue. Identify unsupported search, authorization, or workflow requirements.
>
>
> Acceptance criteria: readers receive only authorized published revisions; edits cannot change published answers; publication verifies approval and updates the published reference atomically.


Generated screens and logic require verification before use. A successful preview does not prove authorization or publishing correctness.


**Acceptance check:** Readers can locate an answer, and authors can propose a replacement without changing it.


## Step 5 — Build the review and approval workflow


Route updates to the person accountable for their accuracy. A proposed knowledge base approval workflow is **author → reviewer → publisher** , with additional reviewers for higher-risk content.


Define exceptions explicitly:


- **Changes requested:** Preserve the reviewed snapshot and decision; create a successor draft.
- **Rejected:** Retain the rejection and prevent publication.
- **Reviewer absent:** Route to an authorized delegate.
- **Overdue:** Escalate to the owner; never silently approve.
- **Approved snapshot needs correction:** Create a new draft; do not transfer the old approval.


Record actor, revision, decision, timestamp, and comments. Record publication separately so approval and release remain distinguishable.


**Make publication atomic.** In one transaction—or an equivalent concurrency-safe operation—verify the publisher’s authority, required approvals for the exact immutable revision, and the expected current published reference, then update that reference and record publication. If any condition changed, fail and re-evaluate rather than overwriting another release.


This prevents a separate “check, then publish” sequence from using stale approval or publication state.


The[Approval Workflow use case](https://www.jetadmin.io/use-cases/approval-workflow?ref=jetadmin.io) describes multi-step routing over existing data with an audit trail. Revision binding, separation of duties, and atomic publication above are recommended controls to implement and test, not demonstrated prebuilt knowledge-base behavior.


**Acceptance check:** Neither a different revision nor a conflicting concurrent release can bypass publication checks.


## Step 6 — Test real questions, access boundaries, and publishing


Use separate accounts for each role and audience. Administrator access can hide permission defects.


Run the questions from Step 1 against known answers. Test navigation labels and alternative wording as well as exact titles.


Then attempt unauthorized and exceptional operations:


- Open drafts through direct links.
- Request another customer organization’s content.
- Retrieve restricted attachments independently.
- Look for restricted titles, snippets, or counts in search.
- Call publishing actions without publisher authority.
- Replace an approved snapshot’s attachment.
- Reject, revise, and resubmit content.
- Attempt concurrent publications.


If AI answers are enabled, verify permission-filtered retrieval and citations. Prompt instructions alone are not an access-control boundary.


### Add a release acceptance checklist


- **Correct answer:** Content matches authoritative sources.
- **Correct revision:** Readers receive the intended approved snapshot.
- **Correct audience:** Current access policies and approved audience scope both apply.
- **Successful workflow:** Rejection, resubmission, approval, and publication work.
- **No unauthorized access:** Direct links, attachments, search, exports, and actions are protected.
- **Safe concurrency:** Conflicting publication attempts fail safely.
- **Traceability:** Decisions and releases identify actors and revisions.
- **Coverage:** Missing answers have an escalation route.


The[Internal Help Desk Software use case](https://www.jetadmin.io/use-cases/internal-help-desk-software?ref=jetadmin.io) describes common answers at intake, owner routing, and record-level HR privacy. Use recurring unresolved requests to identify content gaps without assuming automatic article creation or ticket reduction.


**Acceptance check:** Both permitted actions and deliberate unauthorized attempts behave as specified.


## Step 7 — Publish, schedule reviews, and maintain coverage


Before rollout, verify production connections, identity mappings, access policies, and published content. Assign owners for content problems, access incidents, and publishing failures.


For ongoing knowledge base management:


- Set review intervals according to risk and expected change.
- Trigger review when source policies, products, or processes change.
- Assign overdue reviews to an accountable owner.
- Withdraw unsafe guidance promptly; retain history under your retention rules.
- Provide replacement guidance or an escalation path for retired content.
- Triage feedback into corrections, missing topics, and access issues.


The[Process Automation use case](https://www.jetadmin.io/use-cases/process-automation?ref=jetadmin.io) describes triggers, scheduled jobs, and auditable multi-step processes on live data. Review reminders, overdue checks, and source-change tasks are suggested workflows to configure and test—not established prebuilt features.


Track unanswered searches where search exists, reported inaccuracies, overdue reviews, and approval turnaround. Define each measure consistently; low ticket volume alone does not prove that readers found correct answers.


**Acceptance check:** Every published article has an accountable owner, review trigger, and retirement path.


A useful knowledge base combines clear answers with enforceable access, revision-specific approvals, and ongoing maintenance. Start with one audience and prove the full publishing path before expanding.


[Explore Jet Admin’s Knowledge Base use case](https://www.jetadmin.io/use-cases/knowledge-base?ref=jetadmin.io) and prototype one governed workflow—from proposed change to approved answer.
